sources.title: Psychological price perception may exert a weaker effect on purchasing decisions than previously suggested: Results from a large online experiment fail to reproduce either a left-digit or perceptual-fluency effect
Robustness of Price Perception: How Strong are Anchoring, Left-Digit- and Framing-Effects when Promoting Sales Offers?
The left-digit effect in price and date perception
The leftmost digit change induces a decrease in brain activity related to visuospatial processing: An fMRI study of the price ending effect
Distortion of Price Discount Perceptions: The Right Digit Effect

facts.claim: An online experiment with 266 participants making 4788 purchasing decisions found no support for the left-digit effect.
facts.quote: Against expectations, we found no support for either of the two price-perception effects.

facts.claim: An empirical study in Germany found that psychological factors tested in different experiments have a relatively low impact on the assessment of perceived value for money and cheapness.
facts.quote: it turns out that the assessment of perceived value for money and cheapness for different sales promotion campaigns in Germany (train ticket, smartphone flat rate, filter coffee) is amazingly robust and that psychological factors tested in different experiments have a relatively low impact.

facts.claim: A change in the leftmost digit causes a decrease in brain activity related to visuospatial processing, which may lead to an underestimation of the payment amount.
facts.quote: Our results suggested that a decrease in activity in the regions associated with visuospatial processing suggests that changes in the leftmost digits alter the level of visuospatial attention towards the price, leading to an underestimation of the payment amount.

facts.claim: An experiment showed that when consumers view regular and sale prices with identical left digits, they perceive larger price discounts when the right digits are less than 5.
facts.quote: Consistent with our hypothesized right digit effect, we find that, when consumers view regular and sale prices with identical left digits, they perceive larger price discounts when the right digits are “small” (i.e., less than 5) than when they are “large” (i.e., greater than 5).

facts.claim: A new experiment showed that assuming the first digit of the price is memorized, a round starting price leads to an overestimation of the amount of the offered discount.
facts.quote: Assuming the first digit of the price is memorized, we might expect that a round starting price leads to an overestimation of the amount of the offered discount. The results provide evidence in support of this hypothesis

research.angle: While some brain activity and discount estimation studies suggest the leftmost digit influences perception, large-scale experiments and real-world assessments show these effects are often non-existent or have a relatively low impact.
research.verdict: The evidence is mixed, with some studies showing neurological and cognitive effects of the left-digit while others find no significant impact on actual purchasing decisions.
research.caveat: The results vary significantly between small-scale experimental designs and larger online experiments or real-world assessments.
